query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small fraction (~5–10 at.%) of a stable self-lubricating oxide-forming dopant (e.g., Mo) into a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will form protective tribo-oxides under frictional heat, maintaining a low friction coefficient (~0.2–0.3) and wear rate (~10^−6 mm^3/N·m) from room temperature to 800 °C under typical sliding loads.
generation.material_initial_state: Undoped CoCrFeNi alloy with conventional composition and microstructure, prepared by vacuum induction melting.
generation.intervention: Add a self-lubricating oxide-forming dopant (e.g., Mo) via vacuum induction melting to tailor in situ tribofilm formation during sliding.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests in laboratory air from 25 °C to 800 °C at contact loads up to ~10 N, representative of typical tribological laboratory conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Thermally activated oxide layers formed on the sliding surface, which act as lubricating tribofilms across the wide temperature range.
generation.mechanism: Under friction and elevated temperature, the dopant facilitates the generation of stable, lubricious oxide phases on the worn surface, reducing the contact stresses and preventing severe wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with undoped CoCrFeNi, the doped alloy will exhibit both a lower and more stable friction coefficient and a reduced wear rate throughout the full 25–800 °C range, even as load varies.
generation.baseline: Undoped CoCrFeNi tested under the same conditions, showing higher friction coefficient and wear rate, especially at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Dopant-assisted tribofilm formation is expected to be effective for 25–800 °C in air at moderate loads (up to ~10 N). Performance under higher loads or different environments (e.g., vacuum, humid conditions) remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal dopant fraction and microstructure for maximum tribological benefit are not yet established, necessitating experimental validation. The extent of long-term stability and scalability of dopant design is also untested.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce CoCrFeNi samples with and without ~5 at.% Mo doping in a vacuum induction melting setup. Perform room-temperature to 800 °C pin-on-disk tests under progressively increasing loads (e.g., 2 N to 10 N), measuring the steady-state friction coefficient and volumetric wear.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature and applied load
Wear rate measured by wear track volumetric analysis
Surface chemistry (e.g., oxide species) via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Wear track microstructure (e.g., cross-sectional SEM/TEM) to confirm tribofilm characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If doped samples do not exhibit a significantly reduced and stable friction coefficient and wear rate, or fail to develop durable oxide tribofilms at elevated temperatures, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Remarkable wear resistance and wear mechanisms
cited_evidence.text: Figure 3A shows the Vickers hardness and wear rate variations of NiX and Ni3X as the temperature increases from RT to 800 °C. The hardness of NiX and Ni3X gradually decreases from 6.1 GPa and 4.3 GPa at RT to 3.7 GPa and 2.5 GPa at 800 °C, respectively. The high thermal hardness of NiX arises from the solid solution strengthening and the resultant heterostructures [,]. The trend in wear rate of the Ni3X with temperature is similar to that of the conventional alloys. Specifically, its wear rate increases from 1.1 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at RT to 4.2 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 600 °C, but decreases afterward to 2.4 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 800 °C. However, the wear rate of the NiX is basically maintained at the order of (10−7 to 10−6) mm3/Nm over the entire test temperature. In particular, it achieves ultra-low wear at RT (1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm) and 800 °C (9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm). cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Worn Track Morphology and Wear Mechanism
cited_evidence.text: This is also consistent with the previous friction coefficient data and specific wear rate data. The friction coefficient of FG sample is small, and the specific wear rate is low. Under high normal load, with the increase of sliding speed, the main wear mechanisms of the two samples are adhesive wear, oxidative wear, and plastic deformation. Compared with low loading, the phenomena of wear debris, glaze layers, and oxide layers occurred earlier. This indicates that both samples are more prone to oxidation friction under the high normal load. The oxide layer acts as a lubricating layer, resulting in a reduced coefficient of friction on the worn surface. Therefore, in the friction coefficient curve, the friction coefficient of both samples under high normal load conditions is smaller than that of under low normal load. However, the formation of the oxide layer is accompanied by the occurrence of oxidative wear, which leads to the accumulation of wear volume and the increase of specific wear rate. At this point, the oxide layer formed on the FG sample is more resistant to rupture. Therefore, the FG sample shows good wear resistance.
